title: 3-Read Friday #45: Reading, AI, and Intelligence
author: Craig Barton
summary: This issue pairs Barton's personal stake in early reading with two pieces on how teachers should think about AI and intelligence. He opens with Christopher Such's overview of reading instruction, framing his interest through his own two young children and praising Such as the best available voice for combining theory and classroom practice. He then turns to Ben Newmark's skeptical take on AI's role in lesson planning, noting that Barton himself is running a parallel trilogy of posts on the same subject and, while more optimistic than Newmark, concedes the point that past time-saving innovations rarely delivered the promised time savings. He closes with Dylan Kane's overview of intelligence research, which Barton recommends as essential reading for understanding the implications of that research for teaching.
points: Barton frames Such's reading-instruction post through his own parenting, watching his two young children go through the early stages of learning to read.
He explicitly flags disagreement with Newmark's skepticism on AI and planning while still endorsing the post, showing he curates for quality of argument over agreement.
He references his own concurrent 'trilogy' of posts on AI and teacher planning, situating this issue within his broader ongoing AI-in-education project.
He recommends Kane's intelligence-research overview as essential background for any teacher thinking about how ability and learning interact in the classroom.
quotes: With a 5-year-old and a 2-year-old at home, I am obsessed with the process of learning to read.
And there is no one better at distilling both theory and practice than Chris.
I recently kicked off a trilogy of posts looking at AI's role in supporting teachers' planning, so I read Ben's post with interest.
I think I am more optimistic than he is, but the point about all the other innovations that were supposed to save teachers time really hit home.
If you fancy a solid overview of intelligence research and its implications for teaching - and who wouldn't? - Dylan's article is excellent.
